messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Khai Nguyen was 22 when he came for treatment, a college student who had taken a leave from classes after returning from a relief placement in a war zone. He had gone overseas believing he would be useful, the dependable one in a crisis, helping distribute supplies and move civilians through checkpoints. What stayed with him most sharply was not one single explosion or injury he described in detail, but the repeated experience of standing in lines of frightened people under armed supervision, watched by uniformed men while trying to make quick decisions that never felt like enough. He remembered the pressure of military and police presence everywhere, the sense that every movement was being observed, evaluated, controlled. Back in the United States, those moments had not receded into the past. They seemed to wait for him in ordinary settings.

On campus, the sight of a campus police officer or even the dark outline of a security uniform could stop him in place. If he noticed an officer near the student union, or caught himself feeling that someone was watching him in the library, his mind jumped immediately to the same conclusion: he was not safe, and he was not in control. In those moments he became painfully aware of his body, the rush of adrenaline, the tightening in his chest, his scanning of the room, and he had come to believe this reaction itself meant something was wrong in a deeper way. To Khai, his body had become an enemy, reacting as if danger were still present even when he knew, logically, that he was back on a quiet American campus. The presence of authority figures and uniforms also pulled up a more punishing thought—that when things had mattered most, he had failed in his most important role. He was certain he had not been able to stop bad things from happening then, and the fact that he still froze now seemed to prove to him that he remained helpless.

Because of that, his days grew smaller. He started changing routes across campus to avoid the buildings where campus police were usually posted, and if he saw a uniform ahead he would turn around, even if it made him late to class. In seminars he kept his eyes down, avoiding eye contact with other students because the sensation of being looked at was enough to set him on edge. Friends he had known before he left would wave him over in the dining hall, but he began pretending not to see them, telling himself it was easier than enduring the strain of being visible, having to explain himself, or feeling their attention on him. The fewer people he engaged with, the more isolated he became; still, he experienced the avoidance not as preference but as necessity, the only reliable way to get through the day without being overwhelmed by the sense of being watched or by the shock of suddenly seeing a uniform.

Over the following months, the meanings he gave these reactions seemed to make the triggers spread. Since he believed his body could not be trusted and that he was fundamentally unable to prevent harm, he grew exquisitely alert to signs of surveillance and authority. A professor standing too long near his desk, a security guard outside the library, a police car passing the edge of campus—each caught his attention immediately. What frightened him most was not only the image of uniformed control, but what his own response to it seemed to say about him. If his pulse spiked or he felt exposed under someone’s gaze, he took that as evidence that the danger was somehow still active and that he was still the same powerless person he had been there. In this way, the belief that he had failed and remained helpless made him more sensitive to exactly the cues that undid him.

By the time he sought help, Khai had withdrawn from most social contact and was considering dropping another semester because simply walking to class felt like navigating a field of threats. He sat angled toward the door in the intake room and rarely met the therapist’s eyes for more than a second. He said he was tired of planning his day around avoiding campus police, avoiding other students, avoiding the feeling of being observed. More than anything, he feared that this was permanent—that his body would always act as if the war had followed him home, and that this meant he had already failed at the one role that had mattered to him. At the same time, the fact that he came at all suggested a small competing hope: that if someone could help him understand why ordinary people in authority, uniforms, and even another person’s gaze had come to feel so dangerous, he might still be able to return to school and to other people without bracing for harm.
